findings.bill_quote: (5) Using third parties to assess the potential for catastrophic risks and the effectiveness of mitigations of catastrophic risks.
findings.problem: The summary singles out only the third-party topic out of ten required framework topics. A reader could think third-party use is the main content requirement, or that third-party assessment is itself mandated. The bill only requires the framework to describe how the developer approaches using third parties.

findings.bill_quote: A large frontier developer that fails to publish or transmit a compliant document required to be published or transmitted under this chapter, makes a statement in violation of subdivision (e) of Section 22757.12, fails to report an incident as required by Section 22757.13, or fails to comply with its own frontier AI framework shall be subject to a civil penalty
findings.problem: The box says only 'civil penalty on large frontier developers'. It gives no hint that the penalty does not reach frontier developers that are not large, even though the box lists duties on all frontier developers (transparency reports, incident reporting). A reader would likely assume those duties carry the $1M penalty for every frontier developer.

findings.bill_quote: provided that the non-Federal entities submit to the Assistant Attorney General, before undertaking the proposed coordinated delay or limitation, written notice
findings.problem: The notice is a condition of the exemption, not a binding duty. Entities that skip it simply lose the safe harbor. Marking it force "duty" overstates its legal force, and the entry's own registration-row summary admits it is "Not a registration duty".

findings.bill_quote: any non-Federal entity claiming the exemption shall bear the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence
findings.problem: This is an evidentiary burden on a party claiming an affirmative defense, not an obligation imposed on the entity. Labelling it a "duty" and listing it under requires misstates its legal force.

findings.bill_quote: “Frontier developer”, a person who has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model
findings.problem: The box mentions anti-retaliation as binding frontier developers but omits that all frontier developers also carry the transparency-report, incident-reporting and false-statement duties. The 'requires' text does partly cover this.

findings.bill_quote: A large frontier developer that fails to publish or transmit a compliant document required to be published or transmitted under this chapter
findings.problem: The civil penalty in § 5 reaches only large frontier developers. The row does not note that frontier developers that are not large face no stated civil penalty for their duties, such as incident reporting, so the 'yes' could read as covering all covered parties.

items.reason: Sec. 1(c) requires every artificial intelligence company to test all AI technology annually for biases, inaccuracies and cybersecurity threats and report to the Office of Information Technology. It has no frontier, compute, revenue or capability threshold and is not aimed at catastrophic harm, so it falls under general safety-testing and reporting duties on every AI company, which are out of scope.

The bill (Section 4) only directs state departments to study and report on the impact of artificial intelligence on the workforce, which falls under the out-of-scope item of workforce or economic studies; it has no frontier-model, catastrophic-risk or other in-scope provision.

findings.bill_quote: Any document, including in electronic form, or testimony provided to the Board in response to a request under subparagraph (B) shall be-- (i) treated as voluntarily provided; and (ii) subject to the protections set forth under subsection (j).
findings.problem: The entry never states that information given in response to a Board request counts as voluntarily provided and receives the subsection (j) protections. This provision decides when the liability shield and the disclosure exemptions apply.

items.reason: The bill's binding provisions (Business & Commerce Code §§ 552.051-552.057, ch. 553, ch. 554) are general AI-use rules aimed at ordinary harms: consumer disclosure, manipulation to self-harm or crime, social scoring, biometric capture, discrimination, sexual content, plus a sandbox and a council. None is limited by a frontier threshold or aimed at catastrophic harm, and § 552.003 preempts only local ordinances, not state AI laws. This falls under the OUT-list rules that apply to any AI user or deployer with no size, compute or capability threshold, and under sector and use-specific AI rules.
